body:
Why did Gandhi propose Non-Cooperation?

Gandhi argued that British rule in India survived partly because Indians continued to cooperate with its institutions. Indian officials served in the colonial administration, students attended government-controlled educational institutions, lawyers worked in British courts, and consumers purchased imported goods.

In Hind Swaraj (1909), Gandhi had argued that foreign rule depended on the cooperation of those being governed. If Indians withdrew that cooperation in a disciplined and non-violent manner, the colonial system would lose much of its practical support and legitimacy.

Non-Cooperation

Non-Cooperation was the organised refusal to assist or participate in selected institutions and economic activities that supported British colonial rule. It was intended to be a non-violent method of securing swaraj.

The method was more than expressing disagreement. A lawyer leaving a government court or a student leaving a government institution gave up an existing opportunity in order to weaken public dependence on colonial institutions. The success of the programme therefore required personal sacrifice and collective participation.

The main programme

The proposed movement combined the boycott of colonial institutions and foreign goods with the construction of Indian alternatives.

AreaNon-Cooperation measurePurpose
Official honoursSurrender titles and honours awarded by the government.Reject the prestige associated with colonial authority.
EducationBoycott government-controlled schools and colleges; support national institutions.Reduce dependence on colonial education.
Courts and politicsLawyers withdraw from courts; boycott legislative councils and official functions.Withdraw participation from colonial institutions.
Economic lifeBoycott foreign cloth and goods; promote swadeshi and khadi.Support Indian production and reduce dependence on imports.
Social workEncourage Hindu–Muslim unity, the removal of untouchability and temperance.Strengthen social unity and self-discipline.

Boycott means deliberately refusing to purchase, use or participate in something as a form of protest. Swadeshi means favouring goods produced within one's own country. Khadi is hand-spun and hand-woven cloth, promoted as a practical expression of self-reliance.

The programme also proposed withdrawal from the civil services, army and police. Gandhi envisaged a gradual development of the struggle. If the government continued repression, a wider campaign of civil disobedience could follow.

Non-Cooperation and civil disobedience are different methods

Non-Cooperation principally involves refusing cooperation, such as boycotting government institutions. Civil disobedience involves openly breaking an unjust law through disciplined non-violent action. Civil disobedience was contemplated as a possible later stage; the initial Non-Cooperation programme was not simply a call to break every law.

Congress decisions in 1920

The proposal was debated within the Indian National Congress. Some leaders feared that council boycotts would remove opportunities to influence government decisions. Others were concerned that a mass agitation might become violent.

Two Congress sessions were especially important:

  • Special Calcutta session, September 1920: Presided over by Lala Lajpat Rai. The Congress approved Gandhi's Non-Cooperation resolution.
  • Nagpur session, December 1920: Presided over by C. Vijayaraghavachariar. The Congress reaffirmed the programme and committed itself to attaining swaraj through peaceful and legitimate means.

At Nagpur, the Congress also made organisational changes to support wider participation. Provincial Congress committees were reorganised along linguistic lines, and a 15-member Congress Working Committee was established. These changes helped turn the Congress into an organisation more capable of conducting sustained mass agitation.

From a decision to a nationwide movement

Non-Cooperation activity began during 1920, and the combined Non-Cooperation and Khilafat movement developed into widespread mass action during 1921. NCERT identifies January 1921 as the beginning of the major phase of the combined movement.

Gandhi and Shaukat Ali travelled to promote the programme. Students, lawyers, merchants, peasants and other groups participated in different ways. The challenge was to make the boycott effective while maintaining non-violence and building institutions capable of replacing those that had been rejected.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhi explained the dependence of colonial rule on Indian cooperation in Hind Swaraj, published in 1909.
  • Calcutta special session, September 1920: Lala Lajpat Rai presided.
  • Nagpur session, December 1920: C. Vijayaraghavachariar presided.
  • Nagpur reaffirmed Non-Cooperation and established a 15-member Congress Working Committee.
  • The combined movement entered a major phase of mass action in January 1921.
  • Boycott of foreign cloth was associated with promotion of khadi and swadeshi.
  • Trap: Refusing cooperation with a government institution is not necessarily the same as deliberately violating a law.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World—II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 56–59; NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 117–118; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, Special Session Calcutta, 1920, and Nagpur Session, 1920, consulted 21 November 2026; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 9, chapter National Movements in India, printed pp. 28–29, 2016 edition reprinted in 2020.]

pictures.caption: The programme moved from Congress approval to widespread mass action.

title: Non-Cooperation: Its Principle, Programme and Adoption by the Congress

body:
Participation in towns and cities

The Non-Cooperation Movement spread rapidly in many towns during 1921–1922. Students left government-controlled schools and colleges, some teachers resigned, and prominent lawyers abandoned their practices. Lawyers associated with this form of protest included Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das.

People returned government honours, boycotted foreign cloth, and organised demonstrations outside shops selling imported goods and liquor. Demonstrating peacefully outside a shop to discourage purchases is called picketing.

The economic boycott produced a measurable effect. NCERT records that the value of imported foreign cloth fell from approximately Rs 102 crore in 1921 to Rs 57 crore in 1922. This reflected a substantial reduction in demand for imported cloth during the movement.

However, the boycott also faced practical difficulties. Khadi was often more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth, and national educational institutions were not immediately available everywhere. Some students and other participants eventually returned to existing institutions. The strength of the movement varied across regions and social groups.

Peasants and the meaning of swaraj

For many peasants, swaraj meant relief from the everyday burdens imposed by landlords and colonial officials. Participation in the national movement was therefore closely connected with local economic grievances.

  • Awadh, in the United Provinces: Peasants protested against high rents, forced unpaid labour and other demands imposed by landlords. Baba Ramchandra was an important organiser of peasant action.
  • Kheda, Gujarat: Patidar peasants participated in non-violent campaigns against high land revenue demands. They connected their existing local grievances with the wider national struggle.

Begar means forced labour performed without payment. Resistance to begar could become part of a wider protest against colonial authority, even when a local movement had originally formed around a specific grievance.

Tribal participation and its differences from Gandhian methods

In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, tribal peasants opposed restrictions on forest access, grazing and the collection of forest products. They also resented demands for unpaid labour.

The movement associated with Alluri Sitaram Raju was influenced by the wider nationalist atmosphere and supported some Gandhian practices, including khadi and opposition to drinking. However, Raju's followers also carried out armed attacks and guerrilla actions.

This is an important distinction. A local movement could be inspired by Gandhi or use the language of swaraj without following his commitment to non-violence. The Congress did not approve of armed methods as part of its Non-Cooperation programme.

Plantation workers and restrictions on movement

In Assam, tea plantation workers interpreted swaraj as freedom from the restrictions of plantation life. Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, workers could not ordinarily leave plantations without permission.

When news of the movement spread, many workers attempted to leave the plantations and return to their home villages. Their understanding of freedom was closely linked to the right to move and to escape oppressive working conditions. Many were intercepted and faced harsh police action.

Other significant regional connections

  • Punjab: The Akali movement sought to remove corrupt mahants from Sikh gurdwaras. Its campaign became associated with the wider Non-Cooperation atmosphere.
  • Sind: Muslim traders and peasants responded enthusiastically to the Khilafat appeal.
  • Bengal: The Khilafat–Non-Cooperation alliance helped strengthen Hindu–Muslim political cooperation.
  • Madras Presidency: The Justice Party did not follow the general Congress boycott of legislative councils. It regarded council participation as an opportunity to advance non-Brahmin political representation.

What did this diversity reveal?

The movement created a common national platform, but its participants did not all have the same immediate objectives. Students sought educational alternatives, peasants sought relief from economic demands, plantation workers wanted freedom of movement, and many Muslim participants were also concerned about the Khilafat issue.

These differences were both a strength and a limitation. They enabled the movement to attract a wide range of people, but made it difficult to maintain a single programme and consistent non-violent discipline across every locality.

Prelims focus

  • Non-Cooperation gained widespread momentum during 1921–1922.
  • Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das were among the lawyers who gave up practice.
  • Foreign-cloth imports fell in value from about Rs 102 crore in 1921 to Rs 57 crore in 1922.
  • Baba Ramchandra was associated with the Awadh peasant movement.
  • Alluri Sitaram Raju was associated with the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh.
  • The Inland Emigration Act of 1859 restricted the movement of Assam plantation workers.
  • Trap: Alluri Sitaram Raju's armed struggle was not an example of Gandhian non-violent satyagraha.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World—II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 57–61; NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 117–118.]

title: The Spread of Non-Cooperation: Cities, Villages, Workers and Regional Movements

body:
Gujarat as a centre of Gandhian activity

Gujarat played an important role in the development of Gandhi's methods and in the constructive programme associated with Non-Cooperation. The connection is particularly clear in Kheda, Ahmedabad and Gujarat Vidyapith.

Kheda: Land revenue and peasant resistance

In 1918, peasants in Kheda district faced hardship following crop failure and other difficulties. They demanded relief from colonial land revenue collection. Gandhi supported a non-violent campaign in which peasants challenged the demand for revenue that they were unable to pay.

Vallabhbhai Patel became associated with Gandhi's early public work in Gujarat. The Kheda experience demonstrated how peasants could organise collectively around a defined economic grievance.

During the Non-Cooperation period, Kheda's Patidar peasants also took part in campaigns opposing high land revenue demands. The earlier Kheda Satyagraha and the subsequent Non-Cooperation mobilisation were related, but they were not the same event.

Ahmedabad: The labour connection

Gandhi's intervention in the Ahmedabad textile mill workers' dispute in 1918 was another early experiment in organised non-violent action. It showed that satyagraha could address industrial disputes as well as agrarian grievances.

Ahmedabad subsequently became an important centre for promoting khadi, national education and other activities associated with Gandhian politics.

Gujarat Vidyapith and the idea of national education

One difficulty created by the Non-Cooperation programme was that students were asked to leave government-controlled institutions. The movement therefore needed credible educational alternatives.

In Gujarat, this need helped lead to the establishment of Gujarat Vidyapith in Ahmedabad on 18 October 1920 under Gandhi's guidance.

The institution grew from the national education initiative discussed at the Fourth Gujarat Political Conference in Ahmedabad in August 1920. Its aim was to provide education consistent with Indian national aspirations, self-reliance, productive work and service to society.

Gujarat Vidyapith illustrates the constructive side of Non-Cooperation. The movement did not merely ask students to leave an institution; it also encouraged Indians to create institutions that could serve their educational and national needs.

The Ahmedabad Congress session of 1921

The Indian National Congress met at Ahmedabad in December 1921, when the Non-Cooperation Movement was at its height.

Hakim Ajmal Khan presided over the session because the president-elect, Chittaranjan Das, was in prison. Vallabhbhai Patel served as chairman of the Reception Committee.

The session reaffirmed the importance of non-violent mass action and constructive activities, including hand-spinning, communal unity, temperance and the removal of untouchability.

Three distinct Gujarat connections

  • Kheda: Peasant resistance to land revenue demands.
  • Ahmedabad mill dispute: Gandhian intervention in an industrial labour issue.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith: Building a national educational alternative during Non-Cooperation.

The common element was the use of organised public action and self-reliance, but each addressed a different immediate need.

Prelims focus

  • Kheda Satyagraha: 1918, associated with land revenue demands.
  • Ahmedabad mill workers' struggle: 1918.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith was established in Ahmedabad on 18 October 1920.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith was founded under Mahatma Gandhi's guidance.
  • Ahmedabad Congress session: December 1921.
  • Hakim Ajmal Khan presided at Ahmedabad in 1921; Vallabhbhai Patel chaired its Reception Committee.
  • Trap: The 1918 Kheda Satyagraha preceded the nationwide Non-Cooperation Movement.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 116–118; Mani Bhavan Gandhi Sangrahalaya, Satyagrahas of Mahatma Gandhi, entries for Ahmedabad and Kheda, 1918, consulted 21 November 2026; Gujarat Vidyapith, official Journey, entries for August and October 1920, consulted 21 November 2026; Gujarat Vidyapith, official History, founding and educational objectives, consulted 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, Ahmedabad Session, 1921, consulted 21 November 2026.]
